title: Urticaria and angioedema (India)
specialty: Dermatology / Allergy / Internal Medicine / Emergency Medicine

evidenceAudit.scope: Acute and chronic urticaria and angioedema in adults and children in India: recognition, airway emergencies and anaphylaxis, limited investigations, stepwise antihistamine treatment, add-on therapy and referral, built on the ICMR Urticaria and Angioedema STW (July 2022).
findings: Chronic urticaria over 6 weeks, wheals resolve within 24 hours and angioedema within 72 hours, spontaneous and inducible types, C4 and C1-inhibitor testing for angioedema without wheals, limited role of tests, second-generation antihistamines (cetirizine 10 mg, levocetirizine 5 mg, loratadine 10 mg, fexofenadine 180 mg), up to fourfold dose after 2 weeks, add-on cyclosporine 3–5 mg/kg, montelukast 10 mg or omalizumab 300 mg every 4 weeks after 2–4 more weeks, prednisolone 0.3–0.5 mg/kg for up to 10 days, adrenaline 0.2–0.5 mg IM (children 0.01 mg/kg, maximum 0.3 mg) every 5–15 minutes, avoid NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors when drug-induced, and referral criteria checked against the ICMR Urticaria STW (July 2022).

Cetirizine children: 6 months–2 years 2.5 mg once or twice daily (maximum 5 mg/day); 2–5 years 2.5 mg twice daily or 5 mg once daily (maximum 5 mg/day); 6 years and over 5–10 mg once daily (label, Drugs.com).
unverifiedSections: Paediatric cetirizine doses are from the US label (Drugs.com) because the ICMR STW gives none; updosing in children is not covered.

Renal and paediatric doses of levocetirizine, fexofenadine and loratadine are from the US labels (Drugs.com); the STW gives none. Ciclosporin dosing frequency, follow-up intervals and add-on trial durations are general practice.
Use in pregnancy is not covered in the STW.
Bradykinin-mediated angioedema from ACE inhibitors is not classified separately in the STW; antihistamines may not work in it.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Urticaria (hives) is itchy wheals that come and go within 24 hours; angioedema is deeper swelling of lips, eyelids, tongue or genitals lasting up to 3 days. Acute urticaria is usually triggered by infection, drugs (NSAIDs, paracetamol, ACE inhibitors) or food. Chronic urticaria lasting over 6 weeks is usually spontaneous, sometimes inducible by pressure, cold, heat or sun, and rarely needs tests. Treatment is a daily non-sedating antihistamine, increased up to four times the standard dose, then add-on therapy in tertiary care. Throat swelling, breathing difficulty or shock means anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline first. Angioedema without wheals raises the possibility of hereditary angioedema or ACE-inhibitor angioedema. In India, chronic spontaneous urticaria is common in young women, and long courses of oral steroids and sedating antihistamines bought over the counter are frequent and harmful.
keyMechanisms: Mast cell degranulation releases histamine, causing wheals and itch.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria is often autoimmune (antibodies against IgE or its receptor).
Hereditary and ACE-inhibitor angioedema are bradykinin-mediated and do not respond to antihistamines.
Second-generation antihistamines block H1 receptors with little sedation.

symptoms: Swelling of lips, eyes, tongue or throat
Burning or pain with deep swelling (angioedema)
Symptoms worse at night or with heat, pressure or exercise (inducible)
physicalSigns: Raised wheals with surrounding flare, resolving within 24 hours (ICMR STW)
Wheals that fade within 24 hours, leaving normal skin (ICMR STW)
redFlags: Laryngeal symptoms, choking or dyspnoea: emergency (ICMR STW)
Lesions over 24–48 hours with bruising: urticarial vasculitis, refer (ICMR STW)
Angioedema without wheals: hereditary or ACE-inhibitor angioedema
precipitants: Drugs such as NSAIDs, paracetamol and ACE inhibitors (ICMR STW)

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Lesions last more than 24–48 hours, burn rather than itch and leave bruising; refer (ICMR STW), and skin biopsy confirms it.
Grouped itchy papules with a central punctum on exposed skin; history and distribution settle it.
Eczematous, scaly rash limited to the contact site and lasting days; history and patch testing settle it.
Recurrent angioedema without wheals, abdominal attacks and family history; low C4 and C1-inhibitor settle it (ICMR STW).
Angioedema of lips or tongue without wheals in a patient on an ACE inhibitor; history settles it and antihistamines often fail — stop the drug.
Urticaria with breathing difficulty, hypotension or gastrointestinal symptoms after a trigger; clinical diagnosis — give IM adrenaline at once.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Wheals resolve in 1–24 hours; angioedema up to 72 hours.
Fourfold antihistamine after 2 weeks; add-on after a further 2–4 weeks.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Wheals and or angioedema; trigger identified

clinicalManagement.title: Emergency
actions: Airway compromise, choking, wheeze or shock: IM adrenaline 0.2–0.5 mg (child 0.01 mg/kg, maximum 0.3 mg), repeat every 5–15 minutes; refer after stabilisation (ICMR STW; see Anaphylaxis topic).
After angioedema with airway symptoms, oral prednisolone may be started to cover a biphasic response (ICMR STW); observe before discharge.

clinicalManagement.title: First line
actions: Daily second-generation antihistamine (cetirizine 10 mg, levocetirizine 5 mg, loratadine 10 mg or fexofenadine 180 mg) (ICMR STW).
Identify and avoid triggers; stop NSAIDs, paracetamol or ACE inhibitors if they are implicated (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Second line
actions: Still symptomatic after 2 weeks: increase the same antihistamine up to fourfold (ICMR STW).
Review adherence and triggers before stepping up.

clinicalManagement.title: Third line
actions: Tertiary care: add cyclosporine, montelukast or omalizumab (ICMR STW).
Short prednisolone course only for uncontrolled disease (ICMR STW).

clinicalManagement.title: Refer
actions: Refer if uncontrolled on a fourfold dose of cetirizine, levocetirizine or fexofenadine, lesions last over 24–48 hours with bruising, or angioedema does not respond (ICMR STW).
Refer angioedema without wheals for C4 and C1-inhibitor testing (ICMR STW).

vignette.text: Ms F, a 29-year-old bank clerk from Hyderabad, has had itchy red wheals on her trunk and arms almost daily for 4 months. Each wheal fades within a few hours without a mark, and twice her lips have swollen overnight. She has taken prednisolone courses from a local clinic 'whenever it is bad' and chlorphenamine at night, which makes her drowsy at work. She has no breathing difficulty and takes no regular medicines.

guidedApproach.title: Mast cells, histamine and why antihistamines are updosed
guidedApproach.prompt: Why does chronic urticaria respond to higher antihistamine doses?
guidedApproach.guidance: Wheals and angioedema are caused by mast cell degranulation in the skin, releasing histamine and other mediators that make vessels leak. In chronic spontaneous urticaria the trigger is often autoimmune — antibodies against IgE or its receptor activate mast cells repeatedly — rather than an allergy to a food or drug, so extensive allergy testing rarely helps. Second-generation antihistamines block H1 receptors without much sedation, and because the mast cell drive is persistent, higher doses (up to four times the standard) control symptoms in many patients who do not respond to standard doses. Bradykinin-mediated angioedema — hereditary or due to ACE inhibitors — involves a different pathway, which is why antihistamines and steroids do not work for it.

guidedApproach.title: Recognise the emergency and the mimics
guidedApproach.guidance: First decide whether this is anaphylaxis: wheals with breathing difficulty, throat tightness, hypotension, collapse or gastrointestinal symptoms need IM adrenaline at once. Then decide the type: acute urticaria (under 6 weeks) is often triggered by infection, drugs or food; chronic urticaria lasts more than 6 weeks and is usually spontaneous, sometimes inducible by pressure, cold, heat, sun or exercise. Individual wheals should last under 24 hours and leave normal skin. Lesions that last longer, burn, or leave bruising suggest urticarial vasculitis and need a biopsy. Angioedema without wheals points to an ACE inhibitor or hereditary angioedema.

guidedApproach.title: Why fewer tests are better
guidedApproach.guidance: In most patients the diagnosis is clinical and no tests are needed. Investigations are guided by history and examination: a skin biopsy when lesions persist beyond 24–48 hours or bruise, C4 and C1-inhibitor levels when angioedema occurs without wheals, and infection testing only when the history suggests it. Blood tests are needed before immunosuppressive treatment such as ciclosporin. Thyroid tests, autologous serum skin tests and skin-prick or IgE tests have limited value. Explaining this to patients avoids expensive and unhelpful testing and redirects attention to effective treatment.

guidedApproach.title: The antihistamine ladder
guidedApproach.prompt: How do you treat chronic urticaria step by step?
guidedApproach.guidance: Start a once-daily non-sedating antihistamine — cetirizine 10 mg, levocetirizine 5 mg, loratadine 10 mg or fexofenadine 180 mg — and take it every day, not only when itching. If symptoms persist after 2 weeks, increase the dose up to fourfold. If still uncontrolled after a further 2–4 weeks, specialist care adds omalizumab 300 mg every 4 weeks, ciclosporin 3–5 mg/kg or montelukast 10 mg. Avoid long-term sedating antihistamines and repeated oral steroids; a short prednisolone course (0.3–0.5 mg/kg for up to 10 days) is only for severe flares. Children receive weight- and age-appropriate cetirizine doses. Anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline 0.2–0.5 mg in adults or 0.01 mg/kg (maximum 0.3 mg) in children, repeated every 5–15 minutes as needed.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 29-year-old woman has had near-daily itchy wheals for 4 months, each fading within hours without marks, with two episodes of lip swelling. She uses repeated prednisolone courses and night-time chlorphenamine, which makes her drowsy. She has no breathing difficulty and no other medicines.
boardQuestions.question: What is the best next step?

options.explanation: Repeated oral steroids are avoided; short courses are only for severe flares (ICMR STW).
Allergy tests have limited value in chronic spontaneous urticaria (ICMR STW).

options.text: Daily non-sedating antihistamine such as cetirizine 10 mg, increasing up to fourfold after 2 weeks if needed
options.explanation: Correct. This is first- and second-line treatment for chronic urticaria (ICMR STW).
Omalizumab is third-line in tertiary care after antihistamine updosing fails.

options.text: Increase chlorphenamine to three times daily
options.explanation: Long-term first-generation antihistamines are avoided because of sedation (ICMR STW).

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Use the antihistamine ladder in chronic urticaria.
boardQuestions.keyPoint: Non-sedating antihistamine daily, then up to fourfold; avoid steroids and sedating antihistamines.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 58-year-old man on ramipril for 3 years presents with marked swelling of the lips and tongue for 6 hours. He has no wheals or itch. He is breathing comfortably with SpO2 98% and BP 142/88 mmHg. Antihistamine and hydrocortisone given 2 hours ago made no difference.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most likely cause and key action?

options.text: Chronic spontaneous urticaria; increase antihistamine fourfold
options.explanation: There are no wheals, and antihistamines have failed; this pattern suggests bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

options.text: ACE-inhibitor angioedema; stop ramipril permanently and monitor the airway
options.explanation: Correct. Angioedema without wheals in a patient on an ACE inhibitor, unresponsive to antihistamines, is typical; ACE inhibitors are drugs to avoid (ICMR STW).
Contact dermatitis is eczematous and does not cause tongue swelling.
Allergic angioedema usually comes with wheals or itch and responds to antihistamines.
Bites do not cause this pattern of lip and tongue swelling.

boardQuestions.keyPoint: Angioedema without wheals: think ACE inhibitor or hereditary angioedema; antihistamines often fail.

boardQuestions.vignette: A 4-year-old boy weighing 16 kg has had itchy wheals for 3 days after a viral fever. He is otherwise well, with no swelling of the lips or breathing difficulty. His mother asks for something that will not make him sleepy.
boardQuestions.question: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.explanation: This exceeds the 5 mg/day maximum for a child aged 2–5 years (label).
Steroids are not first-line and the dose and duration are excessive (ICMR STW).
Sedating antihistamines are avoided for regular use (ICMR STW).
There are no features of anaphylaxis, so adrenaline is not indicated here.

options.text: Cetirizine 2.5 mg twice daily or 5 mg once daily
options.explanation: Correct. For 2–5 years the label dose is 2.5 mg twice daily or 5 mg once daily, maximum 5 mg/day.

boardQuestions.educationalObjective: Dose a non-sedating antihistamine correctly in a young child.

patientEducation: Take antihistamine daily, not only when itching.
Avoid painkillers like ibuprofen if they trigger hives.
Seek emergency care for throat swelling or breathlessness.
lifestyleAndDiet: Avoid known triggers; food elimination only if a clear link.
mdtReferrals: Dermatology or allergy for refractory disease (ICMR STW)
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review at 2 weeks and again 2–4 weeks after each step-up; taper once controlled (general practice; the STW gives no schedule).

nodes.text: Breathing difficulty, throat swelling, hypotension or collapse?
Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 0.2–0.5 mg (child 0.01 mg/kg, maximum 0.3 mg), repeat every 5–15 minutes; airway; observe for biphasic reaction; refer after stabilisation
Stop any ACE inhibitor permanently; antihistamines, steroids and adrenaline may fail in bradykinin angioedema; early airway help if the airway is involved; C4 and C1-inhibitor; refer
Individual wheals last over 24–48 hours, burn or leave bruising?
Possible urticarial vasculitis: refer for skin biopsy
Tertiary care: add omalizumab, ciclosporin or montelukast
